extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology, aesthetics, and literary theory interested in humor
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying theoretical/analytic criteria about what humor is, how laughter operates, and what kinds of situations produce humorous response, based on Max Eastman's The Sense of Humor (1921). Useful for analyzing jokes, comic situations, and laughter as a social/psychological phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as social expression of acceptance/pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: To laugh is to say 'Yes.' It is to say 'Good!' 'I agree to your emotion!' 'I am happy to see you!' — laughter (and the smile) is a greeting and a definite affirmation of hospitality and delight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eastman repeatedly treats laughter as a communicative social act comparable to speech: observe laughter as a welcome and social bonding mechanism; treat smiles/laughter as indicators of social pleasure rather than private physiological events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between laughter (acceptance) and scorn/derision (rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is not the same as the curling of the lip in scorn; the temper of these two acts is opposite. Scorn, sneer, gibe, jeer, sarcasm, etc., are functions of rejection and are to be dismissed from the topic of laughter at the outset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a comic act, separate 'humorous' laughter (acceptance/delight) from cynical or derisive expressions; do not conflate sarcastic or sardonic responses with the essence of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter evolved as social utility/cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter, after speech, is the chief thing that holds society together; it appears to be intrinsic to the gregarious instinct and signals that individuals are 'more than merely restive in solitude.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret laughter in social contexts as performing bonding or affiliative functions; consider evolutionary/functional explanations when evaluating why a humorous episode 'works' socially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smile/laughter suited to multimodal social communication
rubrics_metrics.description: A smile is luminous and mingles with speech and vision; laughter is an addition of breath, voice and gesture to the smile. Its form fits human conversational needs as opposed to other animals' signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing comic performance, note the integration of facial expression, voice, and gesture: humor that leverages multimodal signals aligns with the communicative role Eastman describes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play as the root attitude of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: The condition in which joyful laughter most continually occurs is that of play; play is an attitude in which instincts are exercised superficially and pleasures are obtained easily — playfulness underlies humorous response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a situation evokes a 'play-attitude' (spontaneous, instinctive, not deliberate pursuit of an end). Humor frequently depends on perceiving events as part of a playful frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playful failure/disappointment produces humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Play is such that success is fun, but failure is funny — humorous laughter often greets failures or disappointments in play; failure becomes an object of amusement rather than distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In judging jokes or comic scenes, look for an element where an expected pleasurable outcome is thwarted in a playful way (e.g., driving a tack into one's thumb) — that structural disappointment often generates the comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tickling and playful pain as primitive model of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Tickling — an experience where something that ought to be painful becomes amusing in play — is the crude and elementary form of play and provides the first picture of what humor is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tickling as a paradigmatic example when analyzing humor that mixes mild threat/pain and delight; note Eastman's claims (cannot tickle oneself; tickling requires social play) as diagnostic features of such comic moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as an instinct/innate capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a humorous instinct present from early in life (Eastman locates the smile/laughter origin ~fortieth day); the instinct makes playful shocks and disappointments yield amusement rather than suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat humor not merely as learned wit but as having an instinctive basis: analyses should consider developmental evidence and infant behavior as relevant to what counts as basic humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funny as midpoint between play and perplexity (surprise/disappointment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary English word 'funny' stands in a mid-position between play and perplexity: situations that are unexpectedly baffling or lightly troubling (not too distressing) are called funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify elements of surprise, incongruity, or benign perplexity when evaluating humor; comic effect often requires the stimulus to be unexpected but not threatening beyond play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as a protective/compensatory device (making best of a bad thing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor functions as a 'little shock-absorber' or instinct for making the best of a bad thing — it preserves digestion, patience, persistence, and inward resilience in the face of trivial but constant disappointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess comic responses for their adaptive/regulatory role: effective humor often reframes setbacks so they become tolerable or even pleasurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interchange/mixture of emotional responses in comic states
rubrics_metrics.description: There is frequent interchange between laughter and weeping; intense emotions can produce spasms of laughter at shocks and sobs at peaks of delight. Slight internal accidents can divert feeling from one channel to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to mixed affect in humorous contexts (e.g., bittersweet or hysteric laughter); such mixtures can be diagnostic of deeper comic attitudes (play vs. pathos).

rubrics_metrics.name: Playfulness is instinctive, not merely deliberate pursuit of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical definitions that treat play as activity undertaken for pleasure are inadequate: elementary play is instinctive and spontaneous, characterized by easy accessibility of pleasure rather than by conscious pursuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether an activity or utterance is genuinely humorous, differentiate spontaneous/playful contexts from consciously manufactured attempts at humor; authenticity of play matters for the comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor presupposes social framing — cannot fully occur in solitary, deliberate contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Many forms of the comic (e.g., tickling) require social interaction; one cannot really tickle oneself and expect genuine laughter because the essence of the game is social.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate humor with attention to social frame and mutual recognition of play; isolated or self-directed attempts often lack the necessary conditions for authentic humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as philosophic/skeptical disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Those whose temperament inclines to humor tend to a sceptical, wistful seriousness when gaiety fails; humorists are often disillusioned yet resilient, seeing values as deriving from whims and thus maintaining skeptical composure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In literary or character analysis, treat comic voice as carrying a skeptical/reflective stance rather than mere frivolity; 'good' humor may include a contemplative or ironic appraisal of values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor often depends on benignity — not genuinely harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is not an act of rejection but of acceptance; even where pain or failure is involved, the humorous reaction treats it as non-serious, benign, or game-like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish benign humor (eliciting laughter without cruelty) from hostile or malicious 'humor' (which Eastman excludes from true laughter); evaluate whether the comic situation preserves the dignity/safety of those involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and cultural-historical signals influence what is judged funny
rubrics_metrics.description: Eastman traces how words like 'fun' and 'funny' evolved and how literary figures (e.g., Rabelais) embody the play-attitude; cultural history shapes the repertoire of what a community accepts as humorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider historical and cultural contexts when applying criteria of humor; what counts as funny in one era or language may not map directly onto another.
